# Results — Study 233 (Shareholder-Yield): total capital return as an equity signal

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). **Shareholder yield = net buyback yield
(year-on-year decrease in diluted shares from SEC EDGAR 10-K)** plus dividend yield. Annual quintile
sort, long the top-20% yielders, short the bottom-20%, aligned to next-year total returns (Yahoo
Finance) for current S&P 500 members (~412 large caps, 2008–2025, survivorship opt-in). Inputs
fingerprint `f1b6fc02e713`.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `WEAK` · Tradability `MIRAGE` · "Shareholder yield predicts outperformance?"  `NOT SUPPORTED`

Shareholder yield — the sum of dividend yield and net buyback yield — is **inverted on large caps**
over 2008–2025. The long-high-yield / short-low-yield hedge lost **−2.8%/yr (Sharpe −0.30, t ≈ −1.3,
hit rate 28%)**. The high-yield quintile (+20.0%) trailed the low-yield quintile (+22.8%) because the
lowest-yield names were the growth/tech winners — exactly the cohort that dominated the post-2009
bull market. The metric is a genuine theoretical improvement over pure dividend yield, but on this
universe and window the sign is backwards. `MIRAGE` to trade.

## Data stamp

- **Universe**: ~412 current S&P 500 members, diluted shares from EDGAR XBRL (~2008–2025),
  annual total returns via Yahoo Finance. Survivorship-biased large-cap cohort (stated).
- **Signal**: net buyback yield (−pct_change in diluted shares). Dividend yield layer available
  but requires a separate yfinance fetch (`--fetch` flag); core results use buyback yield only,
  consistent with EDGAR-only data as in study 64.
- **Fingerprint**: `f1b6fc02e713`

The signal wins in only 5 of 18 years (28%). The last four years (2022–2025) are all sharply negative,
reflecting the growth dominance of low-yield tech names.

## Why the signal inverts on large caps

1. **Low yield = growth winners.** The lowest shareholder-yield large caps are the high-growth tech
   names (FAANG-era) that retained earnings and issued shares via stock-based compensation — precisely
   the market leaders over 2009–2024.
2. **The academic evidence is for broader universes.** Faber (2007) and Boudoukh et al. (2007) test
   shareholder yield on the full market or on value-weight indices. The premium, if any, concentrates
   in smaller, less-liquid names outside the current S&P 500.
3. **Survivorship amplifies the inversion.** Current S&P members exclude the high-yielders that
   delisted (distressed buybacks before bankruptcy) — which would have hurt the long leg.

## The honest takeaway

Shareholder yield is the right theory (total capital return > dividends alone) but the wrong universe
on this tape. On large-cap S&P survivors 2008–2025, the hedge is **−2.8%/yr, t −1.3**, inverted.
Signal `WEAK`, Tradability `MIRAGE`. Not supported as a standalone factor on this cohort.
